newsitem.title: USA: Raytheon pleased with TI approval.
newsitem.headline: Raytheon pleased with TI approval.

text.p: Raytheon Co said it was pleased with the U.S. government's conditional approval of its $2.95 billion takeover of Texas Instruments Inc's defense business, despite being ordered to sell a small component.
"It's a great day for Raytheon," said spokesman Robert McWade. "We're pleased and delighted that Justice has approved this transaction."
The Justice Department required Raytheon to sell Texas Instruments' unit which develops high power amplifier monolithic microwave integrated circuits (MMICs), a small part of the entire deal.
Analysts said they expected the deal to go through but were somewhat surprised that Justice ordered an outright divestiture rather requiring Raytheon to license the technology to competitors.
"Everyone expected approval. I didn't think divestiture would be the answer. I thought they would license it out," said Jack Modzelewski, an analyst with PaineWebber.
Modzelewski said the order to sell the MMIC unit may indicate that that a second Raytheon deal may come under greater scrutiny.

Raytheon is currently in negotiations with the U.S. Department of Justice on its proposed $9.5 billion takeover of the defense business of General Motors Corp affiliate Hughes Electronics Corp's defense business and hopes to wrap up the deal by the fall.
"It seems to be indicated here that there's going to be increased scrutiny," said Jack Modzelewski, an analyst with Paine Webber. "I would say the environment is becoming less and less accomodating."
However, McWade said the government's approval process for the two deals is completely different and there is no relation between the Texas Instruments and the Hughes takeovers.
"There is absolutely no relationship between the two issues," he said.
Roger Threlfall, an analyst with J.P. Morgan, said the Hughes deal would mark the end of major strategic mergers in the defense industry, so naturally it will be under greater scrutiny.
He said Hughes' strength in tactical missiles will be closely examined by the Justice Department. Electro-optical systems and radar could also come under scrutiny, Modzelewski said.

"We think there's substantial competition in all the markets," McWade said. "The most hotly debated has been tactical missiles, and one has to recognize that Lockheed Martin Corp is the leader in tactical missiles," McWade said.
